title: Iraq, Qatar and Kuwait Top IMF 2027 Growth Ranking on Rebound
excerpt: The IMF projects Iraq at 19.0%, Qatar at 18.8% and Kuwait at 17.1% for 2027 — a recovery from deep 2026 contractions that assumes Hormuz shipping normalises from March.
body:
• Iraq (19.0%), Qatar (18.8%) and Kuwait (17.1%) top the IMF's 2027 real GDP growth ranking — but all three are rebounds from projected 2026 contractions of -16.0%, -15.6% and -16.7% respectively.
  • The ranking assumes shipping through the Strait of Hormuz gradually resumes from March 2027 and returns to broadly prewar conditions by October; if it does not, the top of the table does not happen.
  • Outside the rebound group, Guyana is fourth at 16.8% on expanding offshore oil output, followed by Sudan (15.0%), Bahrain (13.9%) and Uganda (9.9%); Vietnam grows 7.5% and India 7.0%.
  • For investors: the benchmark numbers are world growth of 3.4% in 2027 (from 3.1% in 2026), the United States at 2.3%, China slowing to 4.0%, and only three economies — Bolivia, Equatorial Guinea and Haiti — projected to contract at all.

The fastest-growing economies of 2027 will be the ones that shrank most in 2026. Iraq, Qatar and Kuwait lead the global growth ranking for next year, each projected to expand by more than 17%, according to Visual Capitalist's ranking of the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook forecasts. The catch is in the base: the same IMF projections have Iraq contracting 16.0% in 2026, Qatar 15.6% and Kuwait 16.7%, as the Iran war and the disruption of Strait of Hormuz shipping cut energy production and exports. The 2027 numbers are a recovery path, not a boom.

The ranking in full

The top 20 for 2027, in real GDP growth terms: Iraq 19.0%, Qatar 18.8%, Kuwait 17.1%, Guyana 16.8%, Sudan 15.0%, Bahrain 13.9%, Uganda 9.9%, Saudi Arabia 7.9%, Ethiopia 7.8%, Guinea 7.8%, the UAE 7.7%, Vietnam 7.5%, Rwanda 7.2%, India 7.0%, Kyrgyzstan 7.0%, Venezuela 7.0%, Bhutan 6.9%, Benin 6.8%, Tajikistan 6.8% and Niger 6.5%. Five of the top 10 are Middle East economies, which is why the region's aggregate swings from a 0.3% contraction in 2026 to 6.3% growth in 2027 in the Fund's tables. The full country data is published in the IMF World Economic Outlook database.

The arithmetic matters for anyone using the ranking. An economy that falls 16% and then rises 19% ends up roughly where it started — 0.84 multiplied by 1.19 is almost exactly 1.00. Iraq's headline 19.0% therefore represents regaining lost output once energy flows normalise, a different proposition from Guyana's 16.8%, which continues an expansion driven by new offshore oil production rather than recovery from a collapse.

The assumption the whole table rests on

The IMF's 2027 rebound is explicitly conditional. The Fund assumes shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — a route that carried about 20 million barrels of oil a day before the conflict, roughly a quarter of seaborne oil trade — gradually resumes from March 2027 and returns to broadly prewar conditions by October. That assumption also drives the global picture: world growth rises from 3.1% in 2026 to 3.4% in 2027, and emerging and developing economies accelerate from 3.7% to 4.4%. If Hormuz flows recover more slowly, the Gulf rankings, the regional aggregate and part of the global upgrade all move down together.

The large economies tell a steadier story

Below the rebound group, the ranking is a study in divergence. The United States is projected to grow 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by technology investment and domestic demand. India holds at 7.0% in both years on a fiscal-year basis — the fastest rate among large economies — supported by domestic consumption, while Vietnam's 7.5% reflects manufacturing exports. China slows from 4.5% to 4.0%. At the bottom, only three economies contract in 2027 — Bolivia (-1.5%), Equatorial Guinea (-1.0%) and Haiti (-0.5%) — but five G7 members sit in the slowest 20: Italy at 0.6%, France and Japan at 0.7%, Germany at 1.1% and the United Kingdom at 1.2%, against euro-area growth of just 1.2%.

The Fund's wider warnings qualify the optimism. Global inflation is projected at 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% in 2027, public debt in advanced economies rises from 108% of GDP in 2025 toward 115% by 2031, and the IMF estimates just 32 economies now account for 95% of the projected increase in global GDP, down from 54 in its April assessment — growth is concentrating. The 2027 league table is real, but its top line is a war-recovery trade: the economies ranked highest are, in the main, the ones with the most ground to win back.
